brief.situation: 02:15 in the emergency department. You are the nurse for Mr. Petrov, 67, roomed from triage: two days of black, sticky stools and dizziness when he stands. He takes naproxen for his knees and a daily aspirin.
handover: Triage: heart rate 102, blood pressure 124/76, SpO2 97%. ESI 2.

The department's GI bleeding standing order: two large-bore IVs, type and crossmatch with a hemoglobin and coagulation tests, nothing by mouth, crystalloid for hypotension; blood and endoscopy on the physician's order.
The emergency physician is in the department and the gastroenterologist is on call from home.
howItWorks: The clock runs in simulated time; study pace runs three simulated minutes per real minute. Pause any time.
Crossmatched blood takes time to come up, so what you send early matters later.
Partway through you are asked to write what you think is happening. A debrief scores what you did.

parts.label: What
parts.criteria: Upper GI bleeding (black stools then hematemesis) on NSAIDs and aspirin, with a rising heart rate and orthostatic change: hemorrhage progressing toward shock.
parts.modelAnswer: Black stools and now bright red hematemesis on naproxen and aspirin is an upper GI bleed, probably an ulcer. A rising heart rate, orthostatic change and now a falling pressure mean he is heading into shock.

parts.label: Blood and the number
parts.criteria: The restrictive threshold of 7 is for stable patients; an actively bleeding patient's hemoglobin lags behind the loss, so transfuse for the bleeding; two large-bore IVs and the crossmatch early; on his side for airway protection; endoscopy.
parts.modelAnswer: The 7 g/dL threshold is for stable patients. His hemoglobin hasn't caught up with the loss yet, so he needs blood for the bleeding. Two large-bore IVs and the crossmatch early, on his side to protect the airway, and the gastroenterologist for endoscopy.

noProgress.rationale: An active upper GI bleed still in a department room an hour on without endoscopy arranged is harm here.

aspiration.headline: Aspiration
aspiration.body: A patient who may vomit blood lies on his side with the head up and suction at hand, never flat on his back.

shock.headline: Hemorrhagic shock
shock.body: Send the crossmatch early so blood is ready, and transfuse an actively bleeding patient for the bleeding: the first hemoglobin lags behind the loss.

scoped.headline: Resuscitated and scoped
scoped.body: Access and crossmatch early, the airway protected, an early call and blood for the bleeding. That is the expert path.

scopedLate.headline: To endoscopy, with delays
scopedLate.body: Check when access and the crossmatch went in, when the physician heard about the hematemesis and whether blood ran before he left.

time_up.headline: Still bleeding in the room
time_up.body: An active upper GI bleed needs blood and endoscopy arranged within minutes of the hematemesis.

scoring.modelReasoning: Black stools then bright red hematemesis on naproxen and aspirin is an upper GI bleed, likely an ulcer. A rising heart rate with orthostatic change, then a falling pressure, is hemorrhage heading to shock. Two large-bore IVs and the crossmatch go in first so blood is ready; he lies on his side with suction to protect his airway. The 7 g/dL restrictive threshold applies to stable patients; while he is actively bleeding his hemoglobin lags behind the loss, so he is transfused for the bleeding. The physician hears about the hematemesis at once and calls the gastroenterologist for endoscopy.
